html:
The Chumash are an Indigenous people of the southern California coast, from around Morro Bay south to Malibu, and of the northern Channel Islands offshore. They were among the most numerous peoples of California, and lived well without farming.

They lived from the sea. Their great invention was the tomol, a canoe of sewn planks sealed with tar from natural seeps, in which they crossed to the islands to fish and trade. Shell bead money made on the islands circulated widely. Chumash rock paintings in red, black and white survive in caves such as Painted Cave near Santa Barbara.

Europeans first came by sea with Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo in 1542. Lasting change began in 1772, when Spain founded the first of five missions in Chumash land. Mission life, forced labour and disease cut their numbers deeply. In 1824 Chumash at three missions rose in the Chumash revolt, one of the largest Indigenous risings in Mexican California. Their neighbours were the Tongva to the south and the Yokuts inland.
